usage: describing size; 큰 is the modifier form of 크다

에 marks the destination, not the activity
I bought it at the department store
에서 marks where the buying happens
세일 is from English 'sale'; 백화점 modifies it as a bare noun

The department store is big.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 커요.
주말에 백화점에 가요.
I go to the department store on weekends.
에 fixes the destination of 가다.
선물 사러 백화점에 들렀는데 너무 비싸서 그냥 나왔어요.

Real situation: -러 (purpose) + -아서 (so/therefore) chained naturally.

usage: 가까운 is the modifier form of 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular)
에 marks the destination of 가다
I bought it at the supermarket
에서 marks where the buying happens
슈퍼마켓 is usually clipped to 슈퍼 in speech
examples: 슈퍼가 가까워요.
The corner shop is close.
Casual clip 슈퍼 + adjective 가까워요 (가깝다, ㅂ-irregular).
저녁에 슈퍼마켓에서 우유를 샀어요.
I bought milk at the supermarket in the evening.
에서 marks the place of the action 사다.
라면 떨어졌는데 슈퍼 잠깐 다녀올게요.
We're out of ramen, so I'll run down to the shop real quick.
Real situation: -는데 background + -을게요 'I'll (for you)' promise.
nuance: 슈퍼마켓 is a loanword straight from English 'supermarket', and in everyday speech Koreans almost always clip it to 슈퍼 — saying the full 슈퍼마켓 can sound slightly textbook-stiff. Many small 슈퍼 today are also called 마트 on their signs, so the boundary is fuzzy in practice. Register is fully casual-neutral. usage: 조용한 is the modifier form of 조용하다
에 marks the destination of 가다
에서 marks where the studying happens
빌리다 = borrow; the verb that pairs with 도서관
examples: 도서관이 조용해요.
The library is quiet.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 조용해요.
도서관에서 책을 빌렸어요.
I borrowed a book at the library.
에서 marks the place of the action 빌리다.
시험 기간이라 도서관에 자리가 하나도 없더라고요.
It's exam season, so there wasn't a single open seat at the library.
Real situation: -(이)라 'because it is' + retrospective -더라고요.
nuance: 도서관 is Sino-Korean 圖書館, literally 'pictures-books-building' (圖 picture + 書 writing/book + 館 hall), a public place to read, study, and borrow books where quiet is expected. usage: 국립 = state-run; a common fixed modifier
에 marks the destination of 가다
I look around at the museum
에서 marks where the looking happens
입장료 is the cost to enter a 박물관
examples: 박물관이 유명해요.
The museum is famous.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 유명해요.
박물관에서 옛날 물건을 봤어요.
I saw old objects at the museum.
에서 marks the place of the action 보다.
박물관은 월요일마다 쉬니까 미리 확인하고 가세요.
The museum is closed every Monday, so check ahead before you go.
Real situation: -마다 'every' + reason -니까 + command -세요.
nuance: 박물관 is Sino-Korean 博物館, literally 'broad-things-building' (博 broad + 物 things + 館 hall) — a place displaying historical relics, artifacts, and natural specimens so visitors learn about the past. The essential contrast is 박물관 vs 미술관: a 박물관 shows HISTORY and objects (pottery, tools, dinosaur bones), while a 미술관 shows ART (paintings, sculpture). English lumps both under 'museum' (we say 'art museum'), which is exactly why learners wrongly call a painting gallery a 박물관. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 박물관을 구경하다/관람하다, 전시(를) 보다, 입장료를 내다, 국립중앙박물관. The English-speaker pitfall is precisely this 'art museum = 박물관' transfer error, plus the usual motion-particle split: go TO it with 에 (박물관에 가다) but view things THERE with 에서 (박물관에서 보다).

I go to the art gallery
에 marks the destination of 가다

The art gallery is quiet.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 조용해요.

에서 marks the place; 못 + verb = cannot.
이번 전시는 인기가 많아서 미술관 앞에 줄이 엄청 길었어요.

usage: 가까운 is the modifier form of 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular)
다니다 = attend regularly; the verb that pairs with 교회
에서 marks where the praying happens
common way to ask about someone's faith
examples: 교회가 커요.
The church is big.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 커요.
일요일마다 교회에 가요.
I go to church every Sunday.
-마다 = every; 에 marks the destination.
저는 모태신앙이라 어릴 때부터 교회에 다녔어요.
I was born into the faith, so I've gone to church since I was little.
Real situation: -(이)라 'because it is' + 부터 'from/since'.

The English-speaker pitfall is the Protestant/Catholic blur (교회 vs 성당) plus saying 교회에서 가요 instead of the motion-correct 교회에 가요.

usage: 산속 (deep in the mountains) is a typical setting for 절
에 marks the destination of 가다
에서 marks where the praying happens
오래된 (long-standing) is the modifier of 오래되다
examples: 절이 조용해요.
The temple is quiet.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 조용해요.
새해에 절에서 소원을 빌었어요.
I made a wish at the temple for the new year.
에서 marks the place; 소원을 빌다 = make a wish.

usage: place name + 시청; also a famous subway stop
에 marks the destination of 가다
I handle business at city hall
일을 보다 = take care of official business
examples: 시청이 커요.
City hall is big.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 커요.
시청에서 서류를 받았어요.
I received documents at city hall.
에서 marks the place of the action 받다.
그건 구청 소관이라 시청까지 갈 필요는 없어요.
That's the district office's jurisdiction, so there's no need to go all the way to city hall.
Real situation: 소관(이)라 'because it's the domain of' + 까지 'all the way to'.
nuance: 시청 is Sino-Korean 市廳, literally 'city-government-office' (市 city + 廳 administrative office) — the headquarters of a city government handling major public services. The administrative ladder learners must place it on is the key contrast: 시청 (city hall) > 구청 (district/ward office, 區廳) > 주민센터/동사무소 (neighborhood office). Everyday paperwork (resident registration, certificates) is usually done at the 주민센터, NOT the 시청, so newcomers waste a trip by going straight to 시청. I go to the community center
에 marks the destination of 가다
I apply at the community center
에서 marks where the applying happens

The community office is close.

주민센터에서 등본을 뗐어요.
I got my residence certificate at the community center.
에서 marks the place; 등본을 떼다 = issue a residence copy.
전입신고는 이사한 날부터 14일 안에 주민센터에서 하셔야 해요.

usage: 가까운 is the modifier form of 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular)
I go to the police station
에 marks the destination of 가다
I report it to the police
신고하다 = report to authorities; the verb that pairs with 경찰서
what to dial for non-urgent help
examples: 경찰서가 가까워요.
The police station is close.
Simple description; 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가까워요.
경찰서에서 분실 신고를 했어요.
I filed a lost-item report at the police station.
에서 marks the place; 분실 신고 = lost-property report.
지갑을 잃어버려서 경찰서에 갔는데 다행히 누가 맡겨 놨더라고요.
I lost my wallet so I went to the police station, and luckily someone had turned it in.
Real situation: reason -아서 + 맡겨 놓다 'leave in someone's care' + -더라고요.
nuance: 경찰서 is Sino-Korean 警察署, literally 'guard-inspect-office' (警 alert/guard + 察 examine + 署 government bureau) — the police station where you report crimes, lost items, or accidents. Two contrasts matter: by scale, the small neighborhood post is a 파출소 or 지구대 (local police box) while the larger district headquarters is the 경찰서; and by service, you call 경찰서 (or dial 112) for crime/police but the 소방서 (dial 119) for fires and medical emergencies. 불이 나면 dial 119, which reaches the 소방서
they get dispatched from the fire station
출동하다 = mobilize/respond; 에서 marks the starting point
소방 (firefighting) + 차 (vehicle); kept at the 소방서
examples: 소방서가 가까워요.
The fire station is close.
Simple description; 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가까워요.
불이 나서 119에 전화했어요.
A fire broke out, so I called 119.
-아서 = so/therefore; 119 reaches the 소방서.
옆 건물에서 연기가 나길래 바로 119에 신고했더니 소방차가 금방 왔어요.
Smoke was coming from the building next door, so I reported it to 119 right away and a fire truck came quickly.
Real situation: -길래 'since (I noticed)' + -았더니 'and then (result)'.
nuance: 소방서 is Sino-Korean 消防署, literally 'extinguish-defend-office' (消 extinguish + 防 prevent/defend + 署 government bureau) — the fire station where firefighters (소방관) and fire trucks (소방차) stand by for fires and rescues. The essential pairing every newcomer must memorize: in Korea you dial 119 for the 소방서 (fires AND ambulance/medical emergencies) but 112 for the 경찰서 (police). So a medical emergency also goes through 119/소방서, not just fires — a point that surprises many foreigners. The natural verb 출동하다 (be dispatched) uses 에서 to mark where responders set out from. Register is neutral/official. Collocations: 119에 신고하다/전화하다, 불이 나다, 소방차가 출동하다, 응급실에 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is dialing 911 (the US number — Korea splits it into 119 fire/medical and 112 police) and assuming 소방서 is fire-only when it also covers ambulances — plus the motion particle (소방서에 가다, 소방서에서 출동하다).

usage: country name + 대사관 names a specific embassy
에 marks the destination of 가다
에서 marks where the applying happens
여권을 발급받다 is the fixed phrase, a key embassy errand
examples: 대사관이 멀어요.
The embassy is far.
Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 멀어요.
대사관에서 비자를 받았어요.
I got a visa at the embassy.
에서 marks the place of the action 받다.
여권을 잃어버려서 대사관에 연락했더니 임시 여권을 발급해 줬어요.
I lost my passport, so I contacted the embassy and they issued me an emergency passport.
Real situation: -아서 reason + -았더니 result + 발급해 주다 'issue for me'.
nuance: 대사관 is Sino-Korean 大使館, literally 'great-envoy-building' (大 great + 使 envoy/messenger + 館 hall) — your home country's main diplomatic mission abroad, which helps citizens with passports, visas, and emergencies. Two contrasts matter: 대사관 (embassy, the main mission, usually one per country in the capital Seoul) vs 영사관 (consulate, 領事館, a branch office in other cities handling consular services); and 대사 (the ambassador, a person) vs 대사관 (the building) — note 대사 is also a homonym for 'line/dialogue' in a script, so context matters. Register is neutral/official. Collocations: 대사관에 연락하다, 여권을 발급받다, 비자를 신청하다, 주한 미국 대사관 ('the US embassy in Korea'). The English-speaker pitfall is going to a Korean 시청 or 주민센터 for passport help — those are Korean local offices, while YOUR passport is handled by YOUR country's 대사관 — plus the motion particle (대사관에 가다 for going, 대사관에서 for actions there).
